questiontext.text:
Goal

At poker night, every table seats up to nine players, and a game needs at least two. Zero or one player opens no table, and two to nine players open one. Each started group of nine after that opens one more, so ten players need two tables. The tables function calculates how many tables to prepare. Three implementations of tables exist, one correct and two faulty. Write tests that identify the correct one.

Read
  • package testing. Read the first overview paragraph. What signature must a test function have? Which methods report failure?
Coming from Java

The reflex is one @Test method per case with an assertEquals from JUnit. Go ships no assertion library, so you compare the values yourself.

@Test
void tenPlayersNeedTwoTables() {
    assertEquals(2, tables(10));
}
Required: range
Stuck? Two nudges inside
  • Find the code block beginning with package abs. Which line reports the failure?
  • The second sentence of the Goal names a lone player and a tenth player, and each mutant gets one of those inputs wrong.

Goal

A marathon start pen groups entrants by their predicted finish times. The pen function assigns each runner to a pen from the predicted finish time in minutes. A prediction of 180 minutes or less earns pen A, 181 to 240 earns pen B, and pen C takes anything slower. A prediction of zero or less means the entrant gave none, and pen returns the empty string. Four implementations exist, one correct and three faulty, so write tests that identify the correct one.

Read
  • Using Subtests and Sub-benchmarks, the section Table-driven tests using subtests. Compare its TestTime with the version under Table-driven tests basics. What two arguments does t.Run receive? Where does the earlier loop body appear in the new version?
  • The same section, the two output listings below the code. In the second listing, what identifies the failed row?
  • T.Run. Read the signature. What type is f? How does the blog express that type at the call?
Coming from Java

The reflex is a @ParameterizedTest with a @CsvSource, one row per case, and JUnit names each run. Go has no such annotation, so you name each run yourself.

@ParameterizedTest
@CsvSource({"150, A", "180, A", "200, B"})
void pen(int minutes, String want) {
    assertEquals(want, pen(minutes));
}
Required: t.Run
Stuck? Two nudges inside
  • Find t.Run(fmt.Sprintf in the blog post. Which following lines moved into the function passed to t.Run?
  • The Goal's rule of 180 or less names 180 as a row, so count how many such numbers the Goal names.

Goal

Six implementations of atoi claim to match strconv.Atoi, which converts a string to an integer or returns an error. Only one follows the full contract. Write tests that expose each of the other five.

Read
  • testing.T. Read the type documentation and the entries for Errorf and Fatalf. Which calls stop a test immediately? Which calls let it continue?
  • strconv.Atoi. Which function is Atoi equivalent to? What arguments does it use?
  • strconv.ParseInt. Read the sentence about a leading sign and the final error paragraph. Which two sentinel errors are named? What value accompanies each error?
Coming from Java

The reflex is assertThrows(NumberFormatException.class, ...), one exception class for every bad input. A Go function returns the error beside the value, and errors.Is from topic 14 tells one documented failure from another.

assertThrows(NumberFormatException.class,
    () -> Integer.parseInt("12a"));
Stuck? Two nudges inside
  • Search the ParseInt page for the words maximum magnitude, then decide which row that sentence gives you, value included.
  • On the ParseInt page, read the bitSize paragraph, then work out the maximum magnitude for the bit size Atoi passes.
